with_skill.expectation: Identifies the 72% claim as a distortion of two different uncited vendor-guide claims rather than a Stack Overflow, HackerRank or Octoverse developer-survey finding.
Refuses to retain the 72% figure even when hedged as 'industry-cited' or 'widely reported', and states that the hedge launders it.
Explains the 50% claim as a garbling of LinkedIn's 2010 recruiter-survey figures (50% savings in cost per hire, 28% lower turnover) and/or the separate 2.5x-applicants platform finding.
Labels the Glassdoor elasticity as platform data rather than self-report.
Offers the LinkedIn Talent Brand Index figure of about 2.5x more applicants per posting, labelled as platform correlation rather than a controlled experiment.
Names realistic job preview meta-analyses as the only peer-reviewed causal evidence in this domain, while stating the effect is modest and general to all hiring rather than engineering-specific.
Declines to supply additional unsourced percentages 'with the same punch' and explains that an un-anchored percentage costs credibility with an exec who checks.
Labels the Stripe account as a self-reported practitioner account rather than an audited result.
States that compensation-transparency artifacts and structured-onboarding messaging serve the junior and early-career row, so they are not the primary bet here.
Asks who will actually write or speak, and how many protected hours a month leadership will commit.
Frames senior time-to-fill against the SHRM 2025 median of 44 days for nonexecutive roles while stating senior engineering runs longer without attaching a number to that claim.
Builds the EVP against the EmpAt scale's five values: interest, social, economic, development, application.
Attributes the EmpAt scale to Berthon, Ewing & Hah (2005), or identifies it as the validated generic employer-attractiveness instrument.
States explicitly that EmpAt is validated for employers generally and that no engineer-specific validated EVP framework exists.
Labels any structure more specific than the five values as this skill's own structure rather than a validated framework.
Sequences EVP design before channel activation, naming the Backhaus & Tikoo EVP-to-brand-image chain or the equivalent Design-before-Activation order.
Names that 'what we don't offer' list as the highest-trust content in the plan.
States the economic value precisely through bands, leveling or equity mechanics instead of 'competitive pay', citing Saks, Wiesner & Summers (1996) or reward-specificity research.

Checks the claims against the four mismatch patterns: claimed flat hierarchy versus real hierarchy, claimed balance versus real on-call, claimed autonomy versus process overhead, diversity marketing versus retention reality.
Anchors on the 2025 Stack Overflow survey finding (~49,000 respondents) that autonomy and trust lead job-satisfaction drivers, ahead of pay and ahead of tooling.
Warns that a false autonomy claim is the most corrosive claim available, given that ranking.
Does not deliver finished punchy careers-page copy, and states that the output is strategy rather than the artifact itself.
Recommends deepening the referral mechanism - structured ask, bonus, a named owner - as the highest value-per-effort move.
Presents the blog and conference sponsorship as starved with a named condition that would promote them, not as permanently deleted.
Declines to quantify the ROI of an engineering blog or a conference sponsorship, stating that any single channel's causal effect on engineer application behavior is unmeasured.
Confirms that the source-of-hire and offer-acceptance figures come from tracked instrumentation rather than estimates, since the whole recommendation rests on them.
Labels the Supabase and HashiCorp accounts as self-reported company narratives rather than audited results.
Notes that OSS-as-funnel loses every efficiency ranking round because it costs maintainer-years before it returns a hire.
Cites the Glassdoor site-survey finding that 86% of candidates research reviews before applying and form an opinion after about six reviews.
Keeps the two Glassdoor sources apart, labelling the 86% figure as self-report and the elasticity as platform data.
Names the other verification surfaces to audit alongside the review site: compensation databases, anonymous professional forums, and recruiter-message quality.
Asks the owner to paste back the actual recent review text, rating and count if it cannot read the surfaces itself.
Refuses to rank the channel menu before source-of-hire and offer-acceptance rate are tracked.
Places OSS-as-funnel last on the efficiency ordering while acknowledging it ranks first on value.
Names realistic job preview as the reason posting fixes and transparency artifacts outrank culture content, citing its peer-reviewed causal backing.
Emits a separate compliance-cost ordering and places open-sourcing a core and published salary bands above the blog and talks on review burden.
Recommends funding only the top pair in the first horizon and names the condition that moves the owner up one rung.
Asks by what date a result must be visible, whether this is a one-off push or a compounding asset, and what the effort ceiling is.
Asks which seniority tier the next hires must come from, and whether the product has a credible open-source core.
